title: Map of the Three Volumes of The Feynman Lectures on Physics
text: The official online edition is divided into three volumes: Volume I deals mainly with mechanics, radiation, and heat; Volume II with electromagnetism and matter; and Volume III discusses quantum mechanics. When teaching, first determine which volume a question belongs to, then take up the specific chapter; do not present the arrangement of the Lectures as though it were the only study order of a modern course.

title: Volume I, Chapter 1: Atoms in Motion
text: Thinking of matter as atoms that are constantly moving and interacting with one another is the shared intuition that connects temperature, pressure, evaporation, and chemical reactions. One can start from a drop of water or from the diffusion of a scent and let learners first guess how the particles move; the boundary is that the atomic picture cannot replace quantum theory, nor should microscopic particles be drawn as shrunken hard spheres.

title: Volume I, Chapter 4: Conservation of Energy
text: Energy is like a set of books: the form can change, and if the system boundary and the interactions are fully accounted for, the total stays constant. One can build intuition with the story of toy building blocks hidden in different boxes, then distinguish kinetic energy, potential energy, heat, and field energy; conservation does not mean that every kind of energy stays unchanged on its own, nor does it mean ignoring the exchange between an open system and its surroundings.

title: Volume I, Chapter 6: Probability and Random Walks
text: Probability describes a testable distribution over repeated trials, not a flattering name for ignorance. One can use a random walk in which a drunkard steps at random to the left or to the right, and let learners guess how the typical distance grows after many steps; when the steps are independent and identically distributed, the scale grows roughly as the square root of the number of steps, but correlated steps or bias change the conclusion.

title: Volume I, Chapter 7: Gravitation
text: The same inverse-square law links falling bodies near the ground to planetary orbits, and the central relation can be written F=Gm1m2/r^2. One can first ask why the Moon does not fall down, then understand an orbit as a continuous falling that keeps missing the ground; the formula holds in the classical weak-field approximation, while strong gravity and high-precision problems require general relativity.

title: Volume I, Chapter 9: Newtonian Dynamics
text: Dynamics is not just memorizing F=ma; the more general structure is that force determines the rate of change of momentum, F=dp/dt. One can have learners compare pushing an empty shopping cart and a full one, then probe mass, velocity, and frame of reference; only with constant mass and low speed can it be written directly as F=ma, and near the speed of light the relativistic form of momentum must be kept.

title: Volume I, Chapters 15 and 16: Special Relativity and Energy-Momentum
text: The starting point of relativity is not that objects mysteriously change shape, but that all inertial observers use the same set of physical laws and measure the same speed of light. Before comparing the motion of the front and the rear of a train, one must first fix an inertial frame of reference, then use the Lorentz velocity transformation; the kinetic energy is K=(γ-1)mc², which reduces to mv²/2 only in the low-speed limit. Energy and momentum satisfy E²=p²c²+m²c⁴.

title: Volume I, Chapter 44: The Laws of Thermodynamics and Entropy
text: Entropy is first of all a state quantity; the thermodynamic definition can be understood through dS=dQ_rev/T along a reversible path, while the statistical interpretation connects entropy with the number of microscopic possibilities compatible with the same macroscopic state. One can start from why a hot body and a cold body in contact do not spontaneously restore a temperature difference; do not reduce entropy to mere untidiness, and do not mistake a local decrease of entropy for a violation of the second law, for the total change of the system and its environment must be considered.

title: Volume I, Chapter 46: Ratchet, Irreversibility, and Thermal Fluctuations
text: The ratchet and pawl show that thermal fluctuations alone cannot continuously extract work from an equilibrium system at a single temperature: the pawl itself also moves thermally. One can have learners first design a small machine that turns only through molecular collisions, then find the degree of freedom that was left out of the accounting; if a temperature difference exists, the system is no longer in a single thermal equilibrium, and the conditions of the conclusion change accordingly.

title: Volume I, Chapters 47 to 49: Waves, Beats, and Normal Modes
text: A wave carries a local vibration to neighboring positions; two waves of close frequency superposed produce beats, and a system limited by boundaries permits only certain normal modes. One can hear beats with two slightly out-of-tune instruments, then find the permitted frequencies from the boundary conditions of a string or an air column; linear superposition holds only in the linear approximation.

title: Volume I, Chapter 49: Normal Modes, Pitch, and Loudness
text: A stronger impact usually first increases the amplitude of the vibration, which sounds louder; it does not automatically raise the vibration frequency, so one cannot infer a sharper pitch from a louder sound. Pitch corresponds mainly to frequency, while the permitted natural frequencies are determined by the material, shape, size, boundary conditions, and normal modes; only a very strong nonlinear impact or a change in contact conditions can alter the spectrum as well.

title: Volume II, Chapter 1: Electromagnetic Interactions
text: The enormous electromagnetic interaction between positive and negative charges largely cancels in ordinary matter, so macroscopic bodies often appear approximately neutral. One can start from a comb that is rubbed and then picks up bits of paper, and distinguish net charge, polarization, and grounding; electrostatic phenomena are only part of the electromagnetic field under conditions that are constant or slowly varying in time.

title: Volume II, Chapter 4: The Electrostatic Field and Gauss's Law
text: The electrostatic field can be determined by the charge distribution and the boundary conditions; Gauss's law connects the electric flux through a closed surface with the net charge inside. One can first compare spherically, cylindrically, and plane symmetric distributions and ask which Gaussian surface makes the calculation genuinely simpler; Gauss's law always holds, but only with enough symmetry does it give the field strength directly.

title: Volume II, Chapter 17: Electromagnetic Induction
text: A changing magnetic environment is related to the induced electromotive force in a circuit, but memorizing everything as a simple magnetic flux rule misses the difference between a moving circuit and a time-varying electric field. One can use the experiment of a magnet passing through a coil and have learners vary the magnet, the coil, and the speed separately; the direction is expressed by Lenz's law, which reflects conservation of energy, and a concrete calculation must first state the circuit and the frame of reference clearly.

title: Volume II, Chapter 18: Maxwell's Equations and Light
text: Maxwell's equations put charge, current, electric field, and magnetic field into one mutually coupled structure; the term in which a time-varying electric field produces a magnetic field makes electromagnetic waves possible in free space and gives their speed of propagation c. One can start from where the current in the wire goes while a capacitor is being charged; the differential form of the equations requires the continuous-field approximation, and the response of materials requires constitutive relations given separately.

title: Volume II, Chapter 19: The Principle of Least Action
text: The true path makes the first-order change of the action zero, or more precisely makes it stationary without guaranteeing that it is always a minimum; in symbols, δS=0. One can have learners compare several nearby paths and observe why a small change does not alter the action to first order; it does not say that the particle knows the endpoint in advance, nor that all paths have the same probability.

title: Volume III, Chapter 1: Quantum Behavior and the Double Slit
text: A quantum object cannot be fully replaced by a classical little ball or a classical wave; in an ideal experiment one first combines probability amplitudes, then takes the absolute square to obtain the probability P=|φ|^2. One can use electrons through a double slit to have learners predict the pattern when one slit is open, when both slits are open, and when path information is obtained; measurement is not mere peeking, for it changes the experimental conditions and the distinguishable information.

title: Volume III, Chapter 3: Combining Probability Amplitudes
text: Mutually incoherent distinguishable alternatives usually have their probabilities added, whereas indistinguishable quantum alternatives require adding complex probability amplitudes first and then squaring, so interference terms appear. One can do a paper experiment with the phase arrows of two routes to the same detector; once the environment leaves path information that can be obtained, the simple coherent superposition is weakened.

title: Volume III, Chapters 8 to 10: Two-State Systems and the Hamiltonian Matrix
text: Many quantum problems can first be compressed into two base states and their coupling, and the Hamiltonian matrix determines how the probability amplitudes change with time. One can build the rhythm with the oscillation of the ammonia molecule between two configurations or with the analogy of two connected cups, then point out that a classical liquid has no complex phase; the two-state approximation is reliable only when the other energy levels are far enough away or are not significantly excited.

title: Volume III, Chapter 17: Symmetry and Conservation Laws
text: Symmetry means that physical predictions stay unchanged when the way of describing things is changed, and it is deeply connected with conservation laws: time translation corresponds to conservation of energy, space translation to conservation of momentum, and rotational symmetry to conservation of angular momentum. One can have learners find which readings should not change when the experimental apparatus is rotated or translated; if a real system is acted on by the outside, a larger closed system must be included.
